issue: Does a federal offense that can be committed with only recklessness qualify as a 'crime of violence' under the elements clause of 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(3)(A)?

sides.position: A crime involving ordinary recklessness can satisfy the elements clause (use of physical force) and so qualifies as a crime of violence.
cases: United States v. Borden, 769 F. App'x 266 (6th Cir. 2019), cert. granted, 140 S. Ct. 1262 (2020)

sides.position: A crime that can be committed with only recklessness does not qualify as a crime of violence under the elements clause; the minimum-conduct rule requires presuming recklessness.
cases: Bennett v. United States, 868 F.3d 1 (1st Cir. 2017)
United States v. Windley, 864 F.3d 36 (1st Cir. 2017)
United States v. Tsarnaev, 968 F.3d 24 (1st Cir. 2020)

this_court: Recklessness does not suffice under the elements clause, so Dzhokhar Tsarnaev's arson convictions are not crimes of violence under § 924(c)'s elements clause, at least under existing circuit precedent.
quote: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve a circuit split regarding whether a crime involving "ordinary recklessness can satisfy the ACCA's [elements] clause."
cite: United States v. Tsarnaev, 968 F.3d 24 (1st Cir. 2020)
